newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: EU-ASEAN set to agree pact despite rights issues.
newsitem.headline: EU-ASEAN set to agree pact despite rights issues.

text.p: European and Southeast Asian nations were set on Thursday to agree on a plan to broaden ties despite differences over human rights issues such as East Timor and Burma, delegates said.

The 15-nation European Union (EU) and the seven members of the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) would discuss an action plan to boost political, economic, cultural and security ties, they said.

Progress on the plan stalled at preparatory meetings this week due to Portugal's reluctance to deepen ties with Jakarta over Indonesia's occupation of East Timor and the EU's unhappiness about having to deal with Burma as a future ASEAN member.
A draft copy of the final declaration, obtained by Reuters, calls for "deepening political dialogue through frank discussions of sensitive issues" and increased trade between the two regions.

Dutch Foreign Minister Hans van Mierlo, co-chairman of the two-day ASEAN-EU ministerial meeting, said ties could expand to new areas such as the environment, terrorism, crime and drug trafficking in addition to improved trade.
"These days are of vital importance for the future," he said. "If we leave it to the current trends, then we face the possibility that all (this) is going to slow down."
Delegates said the foreign ministers, meeting at an informal dinner on Wednesday night in Singapore, had agreed to "take action" to deepen ties -- as opposed to making a "strong commitment" to do so.
The fact the ministers had chosen the stronger formulation indicated a compromise had been reached on how to handle the contentious issues, they said.

Indonesia invaded the former Portuguese colony of East Timor in 1975 after a civil war following Lisbon's abrupt decolonisation. Up to a third of the population died in the famine and fighting that followed.
Much of the preparatory talks centred on Burma, which has been promised ASEAN membership along with Laos and Cambodia, possibly as early as this year, delegates said.

British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind called Burma's military government, which has cracked down on a pro-democracy movement, "a rather nasty, dictatorial regime" but said it should not be isolated.

The London-based human rights group Amnesty International said on Wednesday political repression and human rights violations in Burma last year were the worst since the suppression of a popular uprising at the end of the 1980s.
Rangoon called the scathing Amnesty report "ridiculous", and dismissed it as propaganda for anti-Burmese organisations.
Burma's membership of ASEAN is particularly vexing because the European parliament has repeatedly warned the European Commission -- the EU's executive -- it would not tolerate dealings with Rangoon.

ASEAN contends its policy of "constructive engagement" with Rangoon is the best way of reforming the regime and Singapore Deputy Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong, in a speech opening the conference, called for such disputes to be left aside.

"The constructive way forward is for both sides to accept these differences and focus on areas of cooperation, not to fixate on individual contentious issues and allow them to undermine the broader relationship," he said.
